records.title: Number systems and divisibility
records.summary: Classify integers, primes and factors before choosing a shortcut
records.body:
## What you will learn
Classify integers, primes and factors before choosing a shortcut. A prime has exactly two positive factors; 1 is neither prime nor composite.

## Key idea
A number is divisible by 3 when its digit sum is divisible by 3. Divisibility by 9 uses the same rule with 9. Divisibility by 4 depends on the last two digits.

## Worked example
Is 372 divisible by 12? A multiple of 12 must be divisible by 3 and 4. The digit sum is 12, and 72 is divisible by 4. So 372 is divisible by 12.

## Avoid this mistake
Divisibility by 3 alone does not establish divisibility by 12.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: Which number is prime?
practice.explanation: 29 has no positive divisors other than 1 and 29. 21 and 39 are composite.

records.title: HCF and LCM
records.summary: Use the HCF for the largest equal grouping and the LCM for repeating events meeting again.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Use the HCF for the largest equal grouping and the LCM for repeating events meeting again.

## Key idea
For two positive integers a and b: HCF(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b.

## Worked example
Two bells ring every 12 and 18 minutes. Prime factors are 12 = 2² × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3². Their LCM is 2² × 3² = 36 minutes.

## Avoid this mistake
The product identity above is for two positive integers, not a general formula for three numbers.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: What is the HCF of 24 and 36?
practice.explanation: 24 = 2³ × 3 and 36 = 2² × 3². Their common prime powers give 2² × 3 = 12.

records.title: Percentages and successive changes
records.summary: Always identify the base quantity: a percentage is a fraction of that base, not an isolated number.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Always identify the base quantity: a percentage is a fraction of that base, not an isolated number.

## Key idea
Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100. A p% increase multiplies the original value by (1 + p/100).

## Worked example
A fee of ₹800 increases by 10% and then decreases by 10%. New fee = 800 × 1.10 × 0.90 = ₹792. Overall change is a 1% decrease.

## Avoid this mistake
Equal percentage increases and decreases do not cancel because their bases differ.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A price rises from ₹200 to ₹250. What is the increase?
practice.explanation: Increase = 50. Divide by the original 200: 50/200 × 100 = 25%.

records.title: Profit, loss and discount
records.summary: Separate cost price, marked price and selling price
records.body:
## What you will learn
Separate cost price, marked price and selling price. Profit percentage uses cost price; discount percentage uses marked price.

## Key idea
Profit = SP − CP. Profit % = profit ÷ CP × 100. Discount = MP − SP.

## Worked example
A bag costs ₹600, is marked at ₹900, and is sold at 20% discount. SP = 900 × 0.80 = ₹720. Profit = ₹120, or 20% of CP.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not calculate profit percentage using the marked price.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

records.title: Ratios and proportions
records.summary: Ratios compare quantities in the same units
records.body:
## What you will learn
Ratios compare quantities in the same units. Convert a ratio into equal-sized parts before dividing a total.

## Key idea
If A:B = m:n and total is T, A = Tm/(m+n), B = Tn/(m+n).

## Worked example
Divide ₹840 in the ratio 3:4. There are 7 parts, each worth ₹120. Shares are ₹360 and ₹480.

## Avoid this mistake
A ratio of 3:4 does not mean the first share is 3/4 of the total; it is 3/7.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: Split 90 in the ratio 2:3. What is the larger share?
practice.explanation: Five parts total. Each is 18, so the larger share is 3 × 18 = 54.

records.title: Averages and weighted averages
records.summary: An average balances a total across a count
records.body:
## What you will learn
An average balances a total across a count. Groups of different sizes need a weighted average.

## Key idea
Average = sum ÷ count. Combined average = (n₁a₁ + n₂a₂)/(n₁+n₂).

## Worked example
Ten students average 60 marks and twenty average 75. Combined average = (10×60 + 20×75)/30 = 70.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not take the simple average of two group averages unless group sizes are equal.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: Four numbers average 18. Their sum is?
practice.explanation: Sum = count × average = 4 × 18 = 72.

records.title: Mixtures and concentration
records.summary: Track the amount of the active ingredient separately from the total mixture.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Track the amount of the active ingredient separately from the total mixture.

## Key idea
Concentration = amount of ingredient ÷ total mixture × 100. When adding water, the ingredient amount stays fixed.

## Worked example
A 20-litre solution contains 30% syrup, so it has 6 litres of syrup. Add 10 litres of water. New concentration = 6/30 × 100 = 20%.

## Avoid this mistake
Concentration percentages do not add directly.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: 10 litres of 40% juice is mixed with 10 litres of water. New juice concentration?
practice.explanation: There are 4 litres of juice in 20 litres of mixture, giving 20%.

records.title: Time and work
records.summary: Translate completion times into work rates
records.body:
## What you will learn
Translate completion times into work rates. Rates add when people work together on the same job.

## Key idea
If A finishes a job in a days, A’s daily rate is 1/a. Together: rate = 1/a + 1/b.

## Worked example
A finishes in 12 days and B in 6 days. Together they do 1/12 + 1/6 = 1/4 of the job per day, finishing in 4 days.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not add the completion times. Check that both people are working for the stated duration.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A takes 10 days, B takes 15 days. Together they take?
practice.explanation: Combined rate = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 job/day, hence 6 days.

records.title: Speed, distance and time
records.summary: Write consistent units before substituting
records.body:
## What you will learn
Write consistent units before substituting. For equal distances, the slower journey takes more time and affects the average more.

## Key idea
Distance = speed × time. km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

## Worked example
Travel 60 km at 30 km/h, then 60 km at 60 km/h. Total distance is 120 km; time is 2 + 1 = 3 hours. Average speed is 40 km/h.

## Avoid this mistake
The average of 30 and 60 is not the average speed for this equal-distance trip.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

records.title: Trains and relative speed
records.summary: To cross an object, a train must cover the combined lengths
records.body:
## What you will learn
To cross an object, a train must cover the combined lengths. Relative speed depends on direction.

## Key idea
Opposite directions: add speeds. Same direction: subtract speeds. Time = combined length ÷ relative speed.

## Worked example
A 180 m train passes a stationary pole at 54 km/h. Speed = 15 m/s. Time = 180/15 = 12 seconds.

## Avoid this mistake
For a platform, include the platform length as well as the train length.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Formulae_Quant.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A 100 m train crosses a 200 m platform at 10 m/s. Time?
practice.explanation: It must travel 100+200 = 300 m. At 10 m/s this takes 30 seconds.

records.title: Simple and compound interest
records.summary: Simple interest uses the original principal each period; compound interest includes earlier interest in the next period’s base.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Simple interest uses the original principal each period; compound interest includes earlier interest in the next period’s base.

## Key idea
SI = PRT/100. With annual compounding, amount A = P(1+r/100)^t. Compound interest = A − P.

## Worked example
₹1,000 at 10% annually for 2 years becomes 1,000 × 1.1² = ₹1,210. Compound interest is ₹210; simple interest would be ₹200.

## Avoid this mistake
Match the rate period to the number of compounding periods.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

records.title: Linear and quadratic equations
records.summary: Translate words into equations and check solutions against the original constraints.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Translate words into equations and check solutions against the original constraints.

## Key idea
A quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 may factor into two linear factors. Substitute candidate roots to verify.

## Worked example
x² − 5x + 6 = 0 becomes (x−2)(x−3)=0. Therefore x is 2 or 3. Both satisfy the original equation.

## Avoid this mistake
A word problem may reject a negative root even when the algebra allows it.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

practice.prompt: Solve 3x + 5 = 20.
practice.explanation: Subtract 5 to get 3x = 15, then divide by 3: x = 5.

records.title: Permutations and combinations
records.summary: Decide whether order matters before selecting a counting formula.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Decide whether order matters before selecting a counting formula.

## Key idea
nPr = n!/(n−r)! for ordered choices without replacement. nCr = n!/[r!(n−r)!] for unordered selections.

## Worked example
Choose two representatives from five students: order does not matter, so 5C2 = 10. Choosing a captain and deputy instead gives 5P2 = 20.

## Avoid this mistake
Selecting a team and assigning distinct roles are different tasks.

## Your next step

records.title: Probability and complementary events
records.summary: Define the sample space and ensure outcomes are equally likely before counting.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Define the sample space and ensure outcomes are equally likely before counting.

## Key idea
P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

## Worked example
For a fair six-sided die, even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6. Probability of an even result = 3/6 = 1/2.

## Avoid this mistake
Independence and mutual exclusivity are different concepts; do not assume either without justification.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Quantitative Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A fair coin is tossed twice. Probability of two heads?
practice.explanation: The equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH and TT. Only HH qualifies.

records.title: Read a data table systematically
records.summary: Read the title, row labels, column labels and units before answering
records.body:
## What you will learn
Read the title, row labels, column labels and units before answering. Separate what is given from what must be calculated.

## Key idea
For a share of total, divide the requested category by the relevant total, not an unrelated grand total.

## Worked example
A training centre has 40 engineering, 30 science and 30 commerce students. Engineering’s share is 40/(40+30+30) = 40%.

## Avoid this mistake
Check whether the table reports counts, percentages, thousands or cumulative totals.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Data Interpretation 1.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A table lists 25 interns and 75 employees. Interns are what share of all 100 people?
practice.explanation: The relevant total is 100; 25/100 × 100 = 25%.

records.title: Bar charts and line charts
records.summary: Use bars to compare categories and lines to follow a series across ordered values such as time
records.body:
## What you will learn
Use bars to compare categories and lines to follow a series across ordered values such as time. Always inspect the vertical-axis scale.

## Key idea
Percentage change = (new − old)/old × 100. A truncated axis can make a small difference look large.

## Worked example
Sales increase from 80 to 100 units. Absolute growth is 20 units; percentage growth is 20/80 × 100 = 25%.

## Avoid this mistake
A steep-looking line does not establish a large percentage increase without axis values.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Data Interpretation 2.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: Output rises from 120 to 150. Percentage growth?
practice.explanation: Growth is 30 relative to 120, so 30/120 × 100 = 25%.

records.title: Pie charts and central angles
records.summary: A pie chart divides one whole into shares
records.body:
## What you will learn
A pie chart divides one whole into shares. Read the legend carefully and check whether shares total 100%.

## Key idea
Central angle = share × 360°. Share percentage = angle/360 × 100.

## Worked example
A department accounts for 15% of a ₹2,000,000 budget. Its allocation is ₹300,000 and its central angle is 54°.

## Avoid this mistake
A pie slice represents a fraction of the stated total; different charts may use different totals.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

records.title: Data sufficiency and multi-step sets
records.summary: Ask whether the information uniquely determines the answer, rather than rushing to calculate a plausible value.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Ask whether the information uniquely determines the answer, rather than rushing to calculate a plausible value.

## Key idea
Evaluate statement 1 alone, statement 2 alone, then both together if needed. Keep conditions separate.

## Worked example
To determine x+y: knowing x=4 alone is insufficient and y=6 alone is insufficient. Together, they determine x+y=10.

## Avoid this mistake
A single possible solution is not enough if other answers also satisfy the conditions.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Data Interpretation 3.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: To determine the area of a rectangle, length is 8 m and width is 3 m. Which information is needed?
practice.explanation: Area = length × width. Both dimensions are needed here.

records.title: Reading comprehension
records.summary: Find the main claim, supporting evidence and tone
records.body:
## What you will learn
Find the main claim, supporting evidence and tone. Base your answer on the passage instead of outside knowledge.

## Key idea
Read the question, locate relevant evidence, and eliminate options that are stronger or broader than the passage supports.

## Worked example
Passage: “The pilot reduced waiting time at two clinics; a citywide trial is planned.” Supported conclusion: the pilot showed improvement in those clinics. It does not prove every clinic will improve.

## Avoid this mistake
Avoid turning “some” into “all”, or correlation into causation.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

practice.explanation: Only the limited claim about some trainees is directly supported.

records.title: Subject–verb agreement
records.summary: Identify the grammatical subject rather than choosing a verb based on the nearest noun.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Identify the grammatical subject rather than choosing a verb based on the nearest noun.

## Key idea
A singular subject normally takes a singular present-tense verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.

## Worked example
“The list of topics is ready.” The subject is “list”, not “topics”, so “is” agrees with it.

## Avoid this mistake
Phrases such as “of the students” can distract from the actual subject.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: VerbalAbility.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The list of books are ready.
The list of books is ready.
The list of books be ready.
The list of books were ready now.
practice.explanation: “List” is the singular subject, so “is” is correct.

records.title: Sentence completion and context
records.summary: Look for contrast, cause, continuation and tone clues before choosing a word.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Look for contrast, cause, continuation and tone clues before choosing a word.

## Key idea
Words such as “although” and “however” signal contrast. “Therefore” usually signals a conclusion.

## Worked example
“Although the problem was difficult, her explanation was clear.” The contrast is between difficulty and clarity.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not select a familiar word if its meaning conflicts with the sentence’s logic.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Basics of Verbal Ability.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: “The instructions were clear; therefore, the team found the task ____.”
practice.explanation: “Therefore” asks for a result consistent with clear instructions; “manageable” fits.

records.title: Sentence correction and clarity
records.summary: Check grammar, parallel structure and meaning
records.body:
## What you will learn
Check grammar, parallel structure and meaning. Choose a correction that preserves the intended meaning without adding claims.

## Key idea
Items in a list should use a consistent grammatical form.

## Worked example
“She enjoys reading, writing and solving puzzles” is parallel. “She enjoys reading, writing and to solve puzzles” mixes forms.

## Avoid this mistake
A shorter sentence is not automatically the correct sentence.

Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

records.title: Percentage and ratio quick reference
records.summary: Revise percentages using their base and convert common fractions to speed up calculations.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Revise percentages using their base and convert common fractions to speed up calculations.

## Key idea
1/2 = 50%; 1/4 = 25%; 1/5 = 20%; 1/8 = 12.5%. For successive changes a% and b%, use multiplier (1+a/100)(1+b/100), with negative values for decreases.

## Worked example
12.5% of 640 equals one eighth of 640, which is 80.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not apply a formula until you have identified the original whole.

## Your next step

records.title: Geometry quick reference
records.summary: Match each formula to the correct shape and distinguish perimeter from area.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Match each formula to the correct shape and distinguish perimeter from area.

## Key idea
Rectangle: area = lw; perimeter = 2(l+w). Triangle: area = base × perpendicular height / 2. Circle: area = πr²; circumference = 2πr.

## Worked example
A rectangle 8 m long and 5 m wide has area 40 m² and perimeter 26 m.

## Avoid this mistake
Area has square units; circumference and perimeter have length units.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

records.title: Arithmetic and geometric progressions
records.summary: Recognize a constant difference for an AP and a constant ratio for a GP.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Recognize a constant difference for an AP and a constant ratio for a GP.

## Key idea
AP: aₙ = a+(n−1)d; Sₙ = n[2a+(n−1)d]/2. GP: aₙ = ar^(n−1). For r ≠ 1, Sₙ = a(r^n−1)/(r−1).

## Worked example
For the AP 3, 7, 11, …, a=3 and d=4. The tenth term is 3+9×4=39.

## Avoid this mistake
Use n−1 steps to reach term n from the first term.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

records.title: Units, rates and sanity checks
records.summary: Dimensional checks catch many errors before you finish a calculation.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Dimensional checks catch many errors before you finish a calculation.

## Key idea
Distance/time gives speed. Work/time gives rate. A percentage is dimensionless. Keep numerator and denominator units compatible.

## Worked example
At 15 m/s for 20 seconds, distance = 15×20 = 300 metres. The seconds cancel.

## Avoid this mistake
Never combine kilometres with metres or hours with seconds without conversion.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: Formulae_Quant.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A worker makes 18 items in 3 hours. Rate?
practice.explanation: 18 items / 3 hours = 6 items/hour.

records.title: Turn a word puzzle into equations
records.summary: Define an unknown, translate each condition, and test the result in the original story.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Define an unknown, translate each condition, and test the result in the original story.

## Key idea
Write one equation per independent condition. Preserve the distinction between a per-person amount and a total.

## Worked example
Three friends each have x tokens. Each spends 2 tokens. Together they now have x tokens: 3(x−2)=x. Solving gives x=3, so the original total was 9 tokens.

## Avoid this mistake
A value for each person is different from the total across all people.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.

practice.prompt: Two friends each have x tokens. Each spends 3; their combined remainder is 10. Find x.
practice.explanation: 2(x−3)=10 gives 2x=16, so x=8. The remainder is 5 each, total 10.

records.title: Ordering and constraint puzzles
records.summary: Translate each clue into a relation, place forced positions first, then test remaining options.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Translate each clue into a relation, place forced positions first, then test remaining options.

## Key idea
“A before B” is an order constraint. “A immediately before B” also fixes adjacency. These are different clues.

## Worked example
Three tasks A, B and C must satisfy A before B and B before C. The only valid order is A, B, C.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not add adjacency or exclusivity unless the clue states it.

## Your next step
Try the checkpoint below before marking this lesson complete. Explain your method aloud, then revisit any step that felt uncertain.
records.sourceNote: Original Codovate teaching adaptation. Topic reference: 400-Puzzles.pdf. Worked examples and checkpoints are newly written and checked; no source answer key is assumed correct.

practice.prompt: A is before B. C is after B. Which order is valid?
practice.explanation: A must precede B, and B must precede C; therefore A, B, C.

records.title: Invariants and parity
records.summary: An invariant is a quantity or property that an allowed move cannot change
records.body:
## What you will learn
An invariant is a quantity or property that an allowed move cannot change. Parity tracks whether a number is even or odd.

## Key idea
Adding or subtracting an even number preserves parity. Adding or subtracting an odd number flips parity.

## Worked example
Start at 7 and repeatedly add 2. Every reachable value stays odd. Therefore 20 is unreachable with only these moves.

## Avoid this mistake
A pattern from a few examples is not a proof; explain why every allowed move preserves the property.

## Your next step

records.title: A clear framework for estimation
records.summary: Clarify the scope, break the quantity into drivers, state assumptions, calculate, and check the result
records.body:
## What you will learn
Clarify the scope, break the quantity into drivers, state assumptions, calculate, and check the result. Estimates are conditional, not measured facts.

## Key idea
Demand ≈ number of users × usage per user per period. Use a range when assumptions are uncertain.

## Worked example
Estimate daily tea cups at a hypothetical campus: assume 2,000 people, 60% drink tea, and 2 cups per tea drinker. Estimate = 2,000×0.6×2 = 2,400 cups/day.

## Avoid this mistake
Do not present an assumed population or usage rate as verified current data.

records.title: Capacity-based estimates
records.summary: Estimate demand from capacity when the number of users is hard to observe
records.body:
## What you will learn
Estimate demand from capacity when the number of users is hard to observe. Distinguish total capacity from occupancy and actual usage.

## Key idea
Occupied room-nights = rooms × occupancy fraction × nights. Multiply by usage per occupied room-night if needed.

## Worked example
A hypothetical hotel has 80 rooms, 75% occupancy and one soap item per occupied room-night. For 30 nights: 80×0.75×30 = 1,800 soap items.

## Avoid this mistake
If one item lasts multiple nights, divide by the appropriate replacement interval.

records.title: Business cases and sensitivity checks
records.summary: Separate revenue and cost drivers, locate the biggest uncertainty, and test how the conclusion changes.
records.body:
## What you will learn
Separate revenue and cost drivers, locate the biggest uncertainty, and test how the conclusion changes.

## Key idea
Profit = revenue − cost. Revenue = price × quantity. A sensitivity check changes one assumption while keeping others fixed.

## Worked example
A hypothetical service sells 100 units at ₹50 with total costs ₹4,000: profit = ₹1,000. At 80 units and unchanged costs, revenue is ₹4,000 and profit is zero.

## Avoid this mistake
A case framework is a guide, not evidence. Label assumptions and ask for missing data.

records.title: Case study: publishing costs
records.summary: Read a complete cost breakdown and solve three source-based questions with checked explanations.
records.body:
## Read the data first
The source pie chart gives these shares of the total cost of publishing a book. They add to 100%. The chart is rebuilt here as a readable table.

| Cost component | Share of total |
| --- | --- |
| Printing | 20% |
| Paper | 25% |
| Binding | 20% |
| Royalty | 15% |
| Promotion | 10% |
| Transportation | 10% |

## Find the total from a part
If printing costs ₹30,600 and represents 20%, total cost = 30,600 / 0.20 = ₹153,000. Royalty is 15% of that total: 153,000 × 0.15 = ₹22,950.

## Turn percentages into angles
A full pie chart is 360°. Royalty occupies 15%, so its angle is 0.15 × 360° = 54°.

## Work backwards from marked price
If a book is marked 20% above cost and marked at ₹180, cost is 180 / 1.20 = ₹150. Paper is 25% of cost, so paper cost per copy is 150 × 0.25 = ₹37.50.

## Source quality note
Only the three questions supported by the checked table are included below. Other questions in the supplied set still need editorial review; an answer option is not assumed correct merely because it appears in a source.
